hypotheses.title: Accountant.distribute() callable by anyone to drain fee tokens
hypotheses.description: The single-argument `distribute(address token)` overload has no access modifier, so any external caller can invoke it. It forwards the entire token balance held by the Accountant to `feeRecipient`. The two-argument overload is protected by `onlyFeeManagerOrRecipient`, but the one-argument version bypasses that check entirely.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes the Accountant holds accumulated fee tokens (e.g., yBOLD or other ERC20s). 2) Attacker calls `distribute(token)` with the token address. 3) The function calls `distribute(token, balanceOf(this))` which transfers the full balance to `feeRecipient`. 4) Attacker can front-run legitimate distribution or grief by forcing transfers at arbitrary times.
hypotheses.impact: Forced/unexpected transfer of all accumulated fees; griefing of fee distribution timing; potential loss if feeRecipient is a contract that mishandles unexpected transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyFeeManagerOrRecipient` (or equivalent) to the one-argument `distribute(address)` overload.

hypotheses.title: Accountant charges 100% performance fee on gains, zero to depositors
hypotheses.description: The Accountant hardcodes `totalFees = gain` (100% performance fee) whenever a strategy reports a gain. The only mitigation is that if the vault's `totalAssets() < totalSupply()` (i.e., there is an outstanding loss), the fee is reduced by the shortfall. This means any positive gain reported by a strategy is entirely siphoned to the fee recipient, leaving vault depositors with zero upside from strategy yield. The comment "Only take fee if there's no loss" is misleading — the fee is taken on every gain, and only reduced when the vault is underwater.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. An untrusted user deposits into the vault. 2. The strategy reports a gain (e.g., from Stability Pool yield). 3. `report()` sets `totalFees = gain` and returns it to the vault. 4. The vault mints/sends the entire gain to the Accountant, which the fee recipient then distributes via `distribute()`. 5. Depositors receive no yield; the fee recipient captures 100% of all strategy profits.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of yield for vault depositors; all strategy gains are captured by the fee recipient. Depositors are economically disincentivized to deposit, and the vault cannot grow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded 100% fee with a configurable performance fee (e.g., a `performanceFee` bps parameter) and only charge it on the net gain after accounting for losses.

hypotheses.title: StakerFactory.newStrategy lacks access control
hypotheses.description: `newStrategy` is `external virtual` with no modifier, unlike `StrategyFactory.newStrategy` which is `onlyManagement`. Any external caller can deploy a new `LV2SPStakerStrategy` and have the factory configure it with the factory's `management`, `keeper`, `performanceFeeRecipient`, and `emergencyAdmin`. The factory also overwrites `deployments[_asset]`, clobbering the canonical deployment record.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `newStrategy(asset, name)` with any asset. 2) Factory deploys a new strategy and sets its roles to the factory's trusted addresses. 3) `deployments[asset]` is overwritten, so `isDeployedStrategy` returns false for the legitimate strategy and true for the attacker's. 4) Any integrator relying on `deployments` mapping is misled.
hypotheses.impact: Spoofed deployment registry; integrators may route funds to attacker-deployed strategies; loss of trust in factory registry; potential fund loss for downstream consumers.

hypotheses.title: Strategy._tend sets starting price with wrong buffer scaling
hypotheses.description: The starting price is computed as `_available * _price / WAD * _bufferPercentage / WAD / WAD`. `_price` is assumed to be 18 decimals (WAD), and `_bufferPercentage` is also WAD-scaled (e.g., 1.1e18 for 10%). The formula divides by WAD three times, which is one too many. The correct formula should be `_available * _price / WAD * _bufferPercentage / WAD`. The extra `/ WAD` makes the starting price 1e18 times too small, meaning the auction will start at a near-zero price. An attacker can then buy the collateral for almost nothing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker waits for `_tend()` to be called (keeper or anyone). 2. The auction starts with a price that is 1e18 times too low. 3. Attacker immediately buys the collateral at the absurdly low price, draining the strategy's collateral for negligible BOLD.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all collateral in the auction; strategy suffers catastrophic loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the extra `/ WAD` so the formula is `_available * _price / WAD * _bufferPercentage / WAD`.

hypotheses.title: No check that fetched price is non-zero or fresh before auction start price
hypotheses.description: `_tend` calls `COLL_PRICE_ORACLE.fetchPrice()` and directly uses `_price` in `setStartingPrice` without verifying `_price > 0`. If the oracle returns 0 (e.g., during initialization or an oracle bug), the auction starting price becomes 0, and any external actor can instantly buy all collateral for ~nothing the moment `kick` is called.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Oracle returns price 0 momentarily (misconfiguration, chain outage, or feed malfunction). 2. `_tend` is called (keeper or public tend trigger). 3. `setStartingPrice(0)` is set and `AUCTION.kick` executes. 4. Any external actor calls the auction buy at zero/negligible cost, extracting all SP collateral for free.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of collateral rewards held by strategy; vault share value collapses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_price > 0` (and reasonable bounds) before calling `setStartingPrice`; revert if the oracle returns 0.

hypotheses.title: Strategy estimatedTotalAssets ignores pending collateral gains
hypotheses.description: The `estimatedTotalAssets` function returns `asset.balanceOf(address(this)) + SP.getCompoundedBoldDeposit(address(this))`, explicitly excluding pending collateral gains from the Stability Pool. This means the strategy's reported total assets understate its true value whenever there are unclaimed collateral gains. An untrusted actor could exploit this by depositing or withdrawing based on the understated value, or by triggering a report that underreports assets, leading to incorrect fee calculations or share pricing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes that the strategy has significant unclaimed collateral gains. 2. Attacker deposits into the vault at the understated share price. 3. Attacker triggers a claim, realizing the collateral gains, which increases the strategy's assets. 4. Attacker withdraws at the higher share price, capturing a disproportionate share of the gains.
hypotheses.impact: Dilution of existing depositors; unfair distribution of collateral gains; potential profit for an attacker at the expense of other depositors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include the value of pending collateral gains in `estimatedTotalAssets` by fetching the collateral gain and converting it to asset terms using the oracle.

hypotheses.title: StakerFactory.newStrategy is permissionless and can deploy strategies with attacker-chosen asset
hypotheses.description: `newStrategy(address _asset, string _name)` has no access modifier, so any external actor can deploy a new `LV2SPStakerStrategy` via the factory. The factory then calls `setPerformanceFeeRecipient`, `setKeeper`, `setPendingManagement`, `setEmergencyAdmin` on the new strategy, and records `deployments[_asset] = strategy`. An attacker can deploy a strategy for an arbitrary `_asset` (including a malicious token) and overwrite `deployments[_asset]`, breaking `isDeployedStrategy` checks and potentially tricking integrators that trust the factory mapping.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `StakerFactory.newStrategy(maliciousToken, "x")`. 2) Factory deploys a strategy with `_asset = maliciousToken` and sets `deployments[maliciousToken] = newStrategy`. 3) Integrators or users who query `deployments` or `isDeployedStrategy` may be misled into interacting with the attacker-controlled strategy. 4) If `_asset` collides with a legitimate asset already deployed, the mapping is overwritten, causing `isDeployedStrategy` to return false for the legitimate strategy.
hypotheses.impact: Spoofed deployments, broken factory bookkeeping, potential user fund loss via interacting with fake strategy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyManagement` (or equivalent) to `newStrategy`, and prevent overwriting an existing `deployments[_asset]` entry.

hypotheses.title: StakerFactory.setAddresses missing onlyManagement modifier
hypotheses.description: `setAddresses` checks `require(msg.sender == management, "!management")` inline, but the check is on the *current* `management` value which is then overwritten. More critically, unlike `StrategyFactory.setAddresses` which uses `onlyManagement`, this function's inline check is functionally equivalent — however the real issue is that `newStrategy` (unprotected) can be used to deploy strategies whose roles are set from these mutable fields. Combined with the missing modifier on `newStrategy`, an attacker can deploy strategies that inherit whatever addresses are currently configured.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls unprotected `newStrategy` to deploy a strategy. 2) The strategy is configured with the factory's current `management`, `keeper`, `performanceFeeRecipient`, `emergencyAdmin`. 3) Attacker now controls a strategy whose management is the factory's management — but the attacker can still call strategy functions that are permissionless (e.g., `claim`, `tend`).
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can create strategies that appear factory-deployed and interact with them in ways that affect the factory's reputation or downstream integrations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyManagement` modifier to `newStrategy`; keep `setAddresses` protected as-is.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor / donation attack via estimatedTotalAssets inflation
hypotheses.description: `estimatedTotalAssets()` returns `asset.balanceOf(address(this)) + SP.getCompoundedBoldDeposit(address(this))`. The idle `asset` balance is included in total assets, so any external actor can transfer BOLD directly to the strategy to inflate `estimatedTotalAssets()` before the first deposit (or between reports). Because TokenizedStrategy mints shares based on `totalAssets`, an attacker who donates before the first deposit can cause the first legitimate depositor to receive zero (or fewer) shares, or the attacker can front-run a deposit to dilute it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until strategy has 0 shares / 0 deposits. 2) Attacker transfers a small amount of BOLD directly to the strategy address (donation). 3) Victim calls deposit; TokenizedStrategy computes shares = amount * totalSupply / totalAssets, but totalSupply is 0 so first-depositor logic applies — attacker's donation becomes the "seed" and victim's shares are diluted or zero. 4) Attacker (or an accomplice) deposits a tiny amount first to capture the inflated share price, then withdraws.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds for the first/early depositors; share price manipulation; attacker can steal a portion of victim deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Exclude idle `asset.balanceOf(address(this))` from `estimatedTotalAssets()` (only count SP deposit), or use a virtual-shares / dead-shares mechanism in the underlying TokenizedStrategy to prevent donation inflation.

hypotheses.title: Auction starting price ignores oracle staleness in oracle-down multiplier logic
hypotheses.description: In `_tend`, the oracle-down detection relies solely on `_isOracleDown` flag and `priceSource()` from `COLL_PRICE_ORACLE.fetchPrice()`. If the oracle returns a stale-but-not-flagged price (e.g., last good price with primary source while the underlying market has crashed), the strategy sets the auction starting price using this stale high price (no 1000x buffer). The auction will then start at a price far above market, and will never be filled, leaving the strategy's collateral stuck in an overpriced auction. Conversely, if the oracle was down, the 1000x buffer multiplier produces an astronomically high starting price which also blocks sales.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Oracle is marked "down" temporarily or reports a stale price with `priceSource() == primary`. 2. `_tend` computes `setStartingPrice` with `_bufferPercentage *= ORACLE_DOWN_BUFFER_PCT_MULTIPLIER = 1000`. 3. Starting price = available * price / 1e18 * (10% * 1000) / 1e18 / 1e18, producing an enormous starting price. 4. Auction cannot be filled; the strategy keeps accruing bad debt exposure. Attackers can also dump BOLD into the pool at favorable terms while SP collateral is stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral rewards locked in an unfillable auction, strategy unable to convert collateral to BOLD, loss from collateral price depreciation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the oracle-down buffer at a sane maximum (e.g., use a bounded multiplier based on actual deviation), and validate reported prices against TWAP bounds before using them in `setStartingPrice`.

hypotheses.title: Unbounded trove iteration in aprAfterDebtChange causes DoS
hypotheses.description: The function fetches ALL sorted troves via `getMultipleSortedTroves(_collateralIndex, 0, _count)` where `_count = sortedTroves().getSize()`, then loops over every trove in memory. Any untrusted user can open arbitrarily many troves (subject only to gas), growing `_count` without bound. Once the trove count is large enough, the loop and the array allocation exceed the block gas limit, making `aprAfterDebtChange` revert permanently.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker opens many small troves on the collateral in question (each trove is cheap and permissionless). 2) `sortedTroves().getSize()` grows. 3) Any call to `aprAfterDebtChange` (used by vault/APR oracles and integrators) now allocates and iterates over the full list, exceeding block gas. 4) Function reverts for everyone.
hypotheses.impact: APR oracle becomes permanently unusable for that collateral; any on-chain consumer relying on it (vault APR reporting, integrations) is frozen. No direct fund loss but a critical liveness break.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the number of troves iterated (e.g., sample a bounded window) or use an on-chain aggregate maintained by the protocol instead of iterating all troves.

hypotheses.title: Accountant.report trusts caller-supplied gain/loss without verifying strategy report
hypotheses.description: `report()` is gated only by `onlyAddedVaults` (msg.sender must be a registered vault), but the `strategy`, `gain`, and `loss` parameters are entirely caller-supplied and never cross-checked against the vault's actual reported values or the strategy's real P&L. Any added vault (or anyone who can get a vault added) can call `report()` with arbitrary `gain` to mint `totalFees = gain` to itself, or with `loss=0` to bypass loss checks. The healthcheck only bounds `gain` against `strategyParams.current_debt * maxGain / MAX_BPS`, which is a per-call cap, not a verification of truth.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or compromises a vault that has been added to the Accountant (or is the vault itself). 2) Attacker calls `Accountant.report(strategy, gain, 0)` with `gain` set to the maximum allowed by `maxGain` (or with `skipHealthCheck` set via `turnOffHealthCheck` if they are feeManager — but even without, the cap is per-call). 3) Accountant returns `totalFees = gain`; the vault then pulls/charges that amount as fees. 4) Repeat each report cycle to drain vault assets as "fees" to `feeRecipient` (or to the vault's own accounting).
hypotheses.impact: Vault depositors' funds are siphoned as fabricated performance fees; incorrect accounting of gains/losses; potential insolvency of the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have the vault pass the strategy's actual reported gain/loss (or have Accountant read `IVault.strategies(strategy)` and compare against the strategy's `estimatedTotalAssets()` delta), and reject reports where the supplied values diverge from on-chain truth.

hypotheses.title: Accountant fee logic can zero out fees but still report gain, mis-accounting vault
hypotheses.description: When `assets < supply`, the code computes `needed = supply - assets` and sets `totalFees = gain < needed ? 0 : gain - needed`. If `gain < needed`, `totalFees` becomes 0, but the vault still receives a `gain` report and will increase `totalAssets` by the gain while the vault remains underwater. The vault's accounting then reflects a gain that was never actually realized as a fee, and the shortfall persists. This allows the vault to report gains that do not improve depositor solvency, and the fee recipient gets nothing while the vault's internal accounting drifts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Vault is underwater (`assets < supply`). 2. Strategy reports a small gain less than the shortfall. 3. `totalFees` is set to 0, but the vault still processes the gain. 4. Vault's `totalAssets` increases by the gain, but `totalSupply` remains unchanged, so the shortfall is reduced but not eliminated. 5. Repeated small gains can be reported without any fee being charged, and the vault's accounting never reflects the true economic position.
hypotheses.impact: Vault accounting drift; depositors may believe the vault is recovering when it is not; fee recipient receives nothing on legitimate gains.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `gain < needed`, either revert or explicitly account for the loss offset in the vault's report so that the gain is applied to the shortfall rather than reported as a standalone gain.

hypotheses.title: Staker strategy distributes rewards but does not account for losses
hypotheses.description: The `_harvestAndReport` function calls `ACCOUNTANT.distribute(address(asset))` to claim yBOLD rewards and then returns `asset.balanceOf(address(this))` as total assets. This ignores any losses that may have occurred in the underlying vault or strategy. If the vault has suffered a loss, the reported total assets will be inflated by the distributed rewards, masking the loss and potentially allowing the vault to report a gain when it is actually underwater. This can lead to incorrect fee calculations and mislead depositors.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Vault suffers a loss (e.g., due to a bad debt event in the underlying Liquity V2 system). 2. `_harvestAndReport` is called, which distributes rewards and returns the current asset balance. 3. The reported total assets include the rewards but do not reflect the loss. 4. The vault's accounting shows a gain or smaller loss than reality, and fees may be charged incorrectly.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect vault accounting; depositors misled about the vault's health; potential overcharging of fees or underreporting of losses.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_harvestAndReport`, compare the current asset balance to the previous total assets and report the net gain or loss accurately, including any rewards distributed.

hypotheses.title: StrategyAprOracle.aprAfterDebtChange ignores _delta sign for positive deltas
hypotheses.description: The function computes `_stabilityPoolDeposits + _delta` where `_delta` is an `int256`. For positive `_delta` (debt increase), this correctly adds to the denominator. However, the check `if (_delta < 0) require(uint256(_delta * -1) < _stabilityPoolDeposits, "!delta")` only validates negative deltas. For positive deltas, there is no upper bound check, and the addition can overflow if `_delta` is large enough (though Solidity 0.8 reverts on overflow). More importantly, the APR calculation `_weightedInterestRate / _totalDebt * _totalDebt / uint256(int256(_stabilityPoolDeposits) + _delta)` simplifies to `_weightedInterestRate / (deposits + delta)`, which is correct, but the intermediate `_weightedInterestRate / _totalDebt` truncates to zero when `_weightedInterestRate < _totalDebt` (i.e., when the weighted average interest rate is below 1e18). This causes the entire APR to return 0 for low-interest-rate scenarios.
hypotheses.attackPath: No direct attack; this is a logic flaw that causes incorrect APR reporting. An untrusted actor cannot exploit it for profit, but it can mislead integrators relying on the oracle.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect APR values returned (0 instead of the true low APR), potentially causing mispricing or incorrect strategy decisions by external consumers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reorder the arithmetic to `_weightedInterestRate * _totalDebt / _totalDebt / (deposits + delta)` or use a single division: `_weightedInterestRate / (deposits + delta)`.
